name: Magnesium
lead: Magnesium (symbol Mg, atomic number 12) is an alkaline earth metal and an essential mineral that is required for about 300 enzymes in the human body and interacts with ATP, DNA and RNA [1][2]. Roughly half of the body's magnesium is held in bone, according to clinical summaries. It supports nerve and muscle function, energy production, blood pressure and glucose regulation, and is obtained from nuts, seeds, legumes, leafy greens and some fruit juices [2]. Magnesium compounds are also used medicinally as laxatives and antacids and to treat eclampsia [1].

As a supplement, magnesium is widely taken for sleep, muscle cramps, relaxation and general bone health. The evidence is strongest for correcting a deficiency. For other uses, systematic reviews describe the evidence as limited or mixed; for sleep, reviews of randomised trials report heterogeneous findings, with one meta-analysis in older adults finding shorter sleep-onset latency [3][6][8]. A meta-analysis of 14 trials examined magnesium and muscle fitness [4].

No published study has tested magnesium for altering facial or jaw structure in healthy adults. Supplements commonly cause loose stools, and people with impaired kidney function can accumulate dangerous levels.

paras: Magnesium salts are used to correct deficiency, as laxatives and antacids (magnesium hydroxide, milk of magnesia), and, as magnesium sulfate, to treat eclampsia and stabilise abnormal nerve excitation [1]. Clinical trials have tested magnesium replacement in critically ill patients, magnesium for post-spinal headache and during scoliosis surgery, and supplementation in chronic kidney disease [23][24][26][11]. A 2021 review covers the biochemistry of magnesium and the social impact of diseases linked to its deficiency [15].

In bone and appearance supplement discussion, magnesium is included as a mineral that influences calcium handling, parathyroid hormone secretion and vitamin D activation, and is incorporated into the surface of bone mineral. This is a skeletal-health rationale; no study has examined magnesium for cosmetic bone change in healthy adults. Magnesium is also taken for sleep and muscle recovery, which people sometimes link to appearance and physique goals.

A 2021 meta-analysis of three randomised trials (151 older adults) found that sleep-onset latency was about 17 minutes shorter after oral magnesium than after placebo, while the authors described the overall evidence as limited [3]. A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomised trials of stand-alone magnesium for sleep described the evidence as mixed, with separate analysis of trials on cramps and restless legs [6]. A 2024 systematic review examined magnesium for self-reported anxiety and sleep quality, noting the supplement's popularity on social media and questioning how far the claims are evidence-based [8]. A trial in adults older than 51 with poor sleep reported improved indicators of magnesium status and inflammatory stress [9]. An open-label crossover trial tested magnesium chloride for depression [10], and a post-hoc analysis examined magnesium with vitamin B6 in stressed adults [12]. A 2024 meta-analysis examined magnesium and cognitive health [7], and a trial of a magnesium L-threonate formula reported improved cognitive function in healthy Chinese adults [14].

A meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials in athletes, untrained adults and older adults or alcoholics assessed magnesium supplementation and muscle fitness outcomes such as strength, power and lean mass [4]. No trial of magnesium for bone outcomes is included in the cited research; its skeletal role is described mainly in physiological terms. A systematic review of supplement bioavailability found that organic magnesium forms appear more bioavailable than inorganic ones and that absorption is dose-dependent, and that all forms can maintain physiological levels in healthy people without a prior deficit [5].

Sleep: meta-analyses and systematic reviews [3][6][8][9] and registered trials of a magnesium supplement for sleep quality and for sleep and cognition in Saudi adults [19][25]. Muscle: a 14-trial meta-analysis [4] and a registered trial of magnesium citrate on hand-grip strength [21]. Mental health and cognition: trials in depression, stress and cognitive function [10][12][14][7]. Cardiovascular and kidney: a randomised trial of magnesium citrate, oxide and sulfate on arterial stiffness [13], the MAGiCAL-CKD trial on vascular calcification in chronic kidney disease [11], and a registered trial on vascular stiffness [22]. Absorption: a registered comparison of oxide and citrate absorption in healthy subjects [20].
No cited clinical trial examines magnesium for jaw, facial bone or other cosmetic outcomes.

Magnesium supplements, particularly oxide and citrate, can cause diarrhoea and abdominal cramping, consistent with the laxative use of magnesium compounds [1]. People with kidney impairment can accumulate magnesium to dangerous levels, and magnesium can interact with certain antibiotics and with bisphosphonates, reducing their absorption. Dietary magnesium from nuts, seeds, legumes and greens is generally considered safe [2].

Magnesium ions are cofactors for ATP-dependent enzymes and bind phosphate groups in ATP, DNA and RNA [1]. In the nervous system, magnesium blocks the NMDA subtype of glutamate-gated channel in a voltage-dependent way, a finding that underpins interest in its effects on neural excitability, mood and sleep [16][17]. For bone, magnesium influences calcium handling, parathyroid hormone secretion and vitamin D activation, and is held on the bone mineral surface as a reservoir.

Magnesium is a shiny silvery-white metal of low density that forms a protective oxide layer in air; important compounds include the carbonate, chloride, citrate, hydroxide, oxide and sulfate (Epsom salts) [1][2]. Magnesium and its alloys have also been studied as orthopaedic biomaterials [18].

Magnesium was first recognised as an element by Joseph Black in 1755, and Humphry Davy isolated the pure metal by electrolysis in 1808; the name derives from the mineral magnesia from the Magnesia region of ancient Greece [2].

Magnesium is among the most commonly taken supplements, sold in many forms including citrate, glycinate and L-threonate, and is popular on social media for sleep and anxiety [8][5]. In physique and bodybuilding forums it is commonly mentioned as an electrolyte important for muscle and nerve function and as part of evening supplement routines, usually alongside zinc, vitamin D or creatine. Industrial uses include lightweight alloys, desulfurisation in steelmaking and pyrotechnics [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, magnesium is discussed as a general-purpose supplement for sleep, energy and recovery, with users sharing forms, combinations and personal outcomes [27][28][29].

claims.claim: Magnesium glycinate with L-theanine and GABA improves sleep, to the point of sleeping very late
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports going to sleep at 1 am and waking at 4 pm after taking magnesium glycinate, L-theanine and GABA, and missing an appointment, in a thread titled as saying the combination will make you wake up late [27].
claims.experts: Systematic reviews of randomised trials of magnesium for sleep report heterogeneous findings, and one meta-analysis in older adults found shorter sleep-onset latency [3][6].

claims.claim: Magnesium oil promotes hair growth or reduces hair loss
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks about magnesium oil for hair growth and hair loss [28].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page do not report trials of topical or oral magnesium for hair outcomes; the evidence they summarise concerns deficiency, sleep, muscle fitness and mood [1][3][4][8].

claims.claim: Magnesium can cure benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread is titled "the magnesium that cured my mothers bppv vertigo", presenting a family anecdote [29].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page do not report trials of magnesium for vertigo; the evidence is described as strongest for correcting a deficiency and limited or mixed for other uses [1][2].
